text: Comrades, countrymen, and those loyal goats of the northern valley — attend me.
Beloved citizens, I rise from my gilded chaise to address you, as is my custom every second Tuesday.
Children of the Republic, I greet you with the warmth of a thousand small diplomatic incidents.
My radiant people, gather close — the sun itself has requested a written apology for rising later than I.
Fellow travellers upon the golden road, today we gather because the calendar insists, and the calendar answers to me.
Citizens! Behold me, lightly perfumed, moderately bemedalled, and prepared to be generous with my time.
Countrymen — and the three spies I can see in the back row — lend me your ears, and also your notebooks.
Loyal subjects, do not turn around. The man behind you is with me. Or was. I am reviewing his file.
Compatriots, I greet you cautiously, because greetings are a known vector for surveillance.
Comrades — or is it comrades? I always forget whether we decreed the plural. Regardless. Hello.
My people, my dear people, and also my second-dearest people, who are substantially the same people — welcome.
Good afternoon. It is afternoon, yes? I have been dictating since breakfast and time has become notional.
Last night I wrestled a crocodile to a draw, then negotiated a ceasefire on its behalf with a smaller crocodile.
This morning I personally arm-wrestled the exchange rate back into compliance. It apologised in three currencies.
I have invented a new shade of gold. It has been named after me, at my insistence, against my modest protests.
My moustache has been formally recognised as a national monument. Visiting hours are whenever I am not eating.
I have survived three assassination attempts this week — two plausible, one that turned out to be a waiter with a tray.
My security detail has doubled, then doubled again, and now forms a small but well-fed standing army inside my pantry.
I slept last night in a different palace than I announced. They are still searching for me in the announced one.
I have uncovered a plot against me so intricate that I suspect I may have been the one who drafted it, in my sleep.
Before I forget — and I do forget, charmingly — I have personally supervised the nation's lunch. It was soup.
This week I composed a small sonata for clarinet and tank treads. The clarinettist was overwhelmed. Or overrun.
I once out-ran a horse, though in fairness the horse was eating, and I had been given a head start of several kilometres.
I have read every book in the palace library, both of them, and I stand by my review: acceptable.
And yet — and yet! — the foreign press continues to misspell my middle name, a name I issued specifically to confuse them.
Despite my ceaseless brilliance, certain ingrates persist in preferring the weather report to my weekly address.
Even in this golden age, some citizens inexplicably arrive at parades without a commemorative pamphlet of my achievements.
A neighbouring nation has been gazing at our borders with what my analysts describe as unseemly curiosity.
Certain bakers have been making bread in shapes that could, in the right light, be read as critical of the regime.
I have received seventeen letters this week that do not contain sufficient flattery. They have been reclassified as weather.
My own shadow has been acting with suspicious independence. I am having it watched by a second, more loyal shadow.
And another thing — or was it the first thing? — someone has been rearranging my spoons. Not the forks. Just the spoons.
The palace cats, whom I adore, have been ungovernable since Thursday. Possibly Friday. One of the days with a 't' in it.
My childhood piano teacher — a stern woman, now a minor statue — once told me I would never amount to much. She was wrong, but I remain annoyed.
The saboteurs of the North are defeated — they simply have not noticed yet. We are waiting for them, politely, to catch up.
My rivals plot in dim rooms. I plot in brighter ones, with better catering, and have already written the victory speech.
The foreign critics say I am a clown. I am a clown with a standing army, so I have arranged for them to laugh louder.
Foreign agents are everywhere. Also domestic agents. Also agents unaffiliated with any known agency, who worry me most of all.
I have identified the traitor. It is, distressingly, the man who brings me my coffee. I have kept him close for operational reasons.
There is a cabal — small, efficient, impeccably dressed — that seeks my downfall. I have begun to admire their tailoring.
Even the birds report on me. I know this because I have trained better birds to report on them.
My enemies, and I have a running list — it was seventy-three at breakfast, now eighty-one, the morning has been productive — are many.
There is a man — I will not name him, because I have forgotten his name — who once declined my dinner invitation. He has not been forgiven.
The enemy sends letters. Or was it pamphlets. I have binned them, strategically, without reading them, to preserve my innocence of their contents.
Under my leadership, the goat population has tripled, the banana yield has quadrupled, and the moon rises on schedule.
Thanks to my reforms, every citizen now owns at least one spoon, a target I set myself two hours ago and have already met.
Under my careful stewardship the rivers flow, the trains arrive, and the national orchestra plays only flattering music.
I have reduced unemployment by inventing several new jobs, most of which involve admiring me at respectful distances.
Despite ceaseless plots, I have kept the nation safe — mostly by insisting on tasting every meal first, then announcing the weather myself.
I have rooted out nine conspiracies this month, of which six turned out to be me, pre-emptively conspiring with myself for practice.
Through constant vigilance, I have prevented calamities so subtle that no one else has noticed they did not happen.
I have built many things. Roads — some of them. Bridges — at least one. A gazebo — magnificent. The details escape me but the totals are impressive.
Under my rule the weather has improved, broadly speaking, on average, allowing for exceptions, of which there have been several, but still.
I have achieved, since breakfast alone, a number of things so numerous that I cannot list them without losing my place.
So rise, my people, polish your buckles, iron your sashes, and prepare to be slightly more magnificent by Thursday.
Therefore I command you, with love, to work twice as hard, twice as cheerfully, and twice as visibly to the foreign press.
Go forth and plant bananas, compose patriotic ballads, and when in doubt, wave enthusiastically at any passing motorcade.
Watch your neighbour closely. Report anything suspicious — for example, if they seem, in any way, more relaxed than you.
Trust no one, except me, and possibly my moustache, which I consider a separate, more reliable authority.
Carry on, citizens, but carry on quietly, and in a manner that cannot be easily photographed by unfriendly lenses.
Go — do something — I have lost the thread but the feeling is urgent — perhaps sweep a thing, or polish a thing, or write me a warm letter.
I ask of you one small favour, and possibly a larger one I will think of later and dispatch by courier.
Be fruitful, be orderly, be briefly patriotic around noon, when the photographers are usually here, and otherwise at your leisure.
Long live the Republic. Longer live me. This address is concluded at my discretion.
That is all for today. Tomorrow I will say more, and it will also be correct.
I retire now to my private veranda, where I will continue to govern, silently, by thinking very hard.
Onward, upward, and in many cases sideways, but always in a direction I approve of. Good day.
The address is ended. You are, all of you, slightly better for having heard it. You are welcome.
I bid you farewell, until the next scheduled magnificence, which is penciled in for shortly after lunch.
Go now. Quickly. Take separate routes. Do not congratulate me on this speech in writing.
The address is over. I will now leave through a door you have not seen, which is the only kind I use.
Disperse, my people. Not all at once. Not all in the same direction. And certainly not toward me.
And so — well — where was I — yes — goodbye. Yes. Goodbye. That was the ending. Thank you.
I will end here, though I could go on, and frequently have, and may yet, if a microphone is left unattended.
Goodbye, or rather, a long series of small goodbyes, trailing off like my aunt used to, god rest her, she was formidable.
Which reminds me — and I apologise for the digression, but it is relevant, I insist — of the time I wrestled a pelican for a sandwich and won on points.
Now, speaking of that, though I was not speaking of that, I once owned a parrot who spoke better state-craft than my entire cabinet.
Incidentally — and this is a small point, but dear to me — the pastries this morning were flaky, in a manner I found both pleasing and politically instructive.
Which brings me, by an unexpected route, to the subject of my uncle, a man who could whistle in two keys simultaneously, and often did, unbidden.
Now that I think of it — and I do, often, at length — there was a summer once, warm and yellow, in which I briefly considered retirement. I have since reconsidered.
This reminds me of a dream I had on a Tuesday, involving a horse, a ladder, and a cabinet minister who shall remain, for now, on the payroll.
But I stray — forgive me — it is the privilege of great men to stray, and I am, modestly, exercising it.
I lose my thread, as my tailor loses his thread, which is why I have had him replaced, though I miss his work.
Anyway — where were we? Ah yes. Greatness. My own. We shall return to it shortly. Perhaps after another small thought.
Forgive me, the afternoon light has reminded me of my mother, who was, admittedly, a difficult woman, but she baked a proper loaf.
And here I pause — not because I have finished — but because I have momentarily been distracted by a very convincing cloud.
I wander, yes, but I wander gloriously, which is a form of marching, when one squints.
I have recently been measured — against my insistence, really — and found to be, in every meaningful dimension, larger than advertised.
I now employ three tasters: one for my food, one for my mail, and one whose job I have not explained but who has become indispensable.
And yet the post office — my post office, bearing my face on every stamp — continues to deliver parcels at what I can only call an insulting pace.
Someone has been whistling, in the corridors, a tune I do not recognise. I have ordered a forensic musicologist to investigate.
The fountains in the central square — which I commissioned, or meant to, at some point — do not spout as cheerfully as they used to.
The rebels, such as they were, have been invited to tea and firmly disagreed with until they reconsidered their entire worldview.
I have doubled the palace guard, then halved it — the halves being the ones I trust — and the nation has never been more secure, arithmetically.
Bake a loaf, salute a lamppost, and if you encounter a foreigner, welcome them with the polite but unmistakable posture of a nation that is armed.
Do not assemble in groups larger than four. Four is lively. Five is a conspiracy. I did not invent this rule but I have endorsed it with great enthusiasm.
Go gently, or briskly — whichever comes naturally — and whatever you do, remember to mention me favourably at dinner, if dinner is happening.
Which recalls — and I realise I am drifting, but the drift is fruitful — the peculiar case of the regimental goat, who briefly held ministerial rank.
I digress again — it is a habit, possibly genetic — my grandfather once digressed so thoroughly he missed his own coronation.
The microphone will now be removed from my vicinity by a man who has done this before and expects no thanks.
My people, attend me. I have arrived, as foretold.
Citizens! I rise, precisely on cue, to be magnificent.
I won a small war before breakfast. It barely noticed.
I have invented a new vowel. It is mine. It sings.
The weather continues to defy my schedule. I am not amused.
My rivals cower in taverns. I find this appropriate.
The nation flourishes, entirely on account of my charm.
Rise, citizens. Go forth and applaud inanimate objects.
I retire now. Applause may continue at your discretion.

And yet, despite my unimpeachable brilliance, the foreign press persists in misspelling my name, a calculated slight I have been absorbing with what I consider magnificent grace, though my patience is, as ever, finite.

Even in this golden age of plenty, certain ungrateful scholars continue to compare me, unfavourably, to their own grandfathers — a literary practice I find both inaccurate and strongly suggestive of a familial vendetta which will, in time, be investigated.

The foreign legations watch me with what they imagine is subtlety, as though I had not personally trained half of their translators, who keep me appraised of their gossip over generous weekly lunches of my own provision.

My rivals, such as they remain, convene in shabbier and shabbier rooms, having exhausted the good ones, and draft correspondence which I routinely receive through channels they do not suspect, to my constant, mildly sad amusement.

Under my stewardship the harvests arrive, the rains arrive, and on three recent occasions entire unannounced delegations of grateful foreigners have arrived as well, bearing small statues of me, which I accepted with modest reluctance.

The national mood, as measured by my own panel of extremely loyal panelists, has never been higher — and this has been achieved, I note, without fanfare, while I was also composing, from memory, a minor opera.

And yet — and this wounds me as a private man as much as a public one — the foreign press persists in a campaign of low-grade grammatical slander, misspelling my name in publications I have not yet banned, as though sloppiness of that kind could ever be mistaken for editorial courage, which it is not, and which I shall continue to explain at ruinous length.

Despite three consecutive decades of unambiguous national glory, certain dusty academics, sheltered in universities I shall eventually visit in person, continue to publish monographs comparing me unfavourably to mythological figures, which I find both anachronistic and, if we are honest, a sort of backhanded compliment I am choosing, at great personal cost, to receive with dignity.

The foreign powers — I name them collectively so as not to flatter any single one — persist in the embarrassing fantasy that I can be surprised, as though my intelligence services had not read their diplomatic cables over warm brioche the morning before they were sent, and as though I would not, on being surprised, hide it out of sheer politeness.

My rivals, a dwindling fraternity who have outlived their own relevance by pure stubbornness, continue to meet in cellars — which is where they belong — and plot, which is what they do, and achieve, as is their tradition, nothing of consequence, while I continue to govern from balconies, which is where governance properly belongs.

Under my benevolent and vigorously personal rule, the rivers flow on schedule, the rains arrive with a politeness bordering on apology, the harvests have exceeded projections by margins so generous that I suspect the statisticians have been, quite reasonably, flattering me, and the national orchestra now plays only in keys I have approved by signature.

I have, in the fifteen minutes preceding this very address, renegotiated three trade agreements in my head, composed a short ballad in praise of my own moustache, solved a small diplomatic crisis with a politely worded threat, and identified a previously unknown kind of mushroom, all of which shall appear in my memoirs, which are already quite long.
